cards.explanation: The answer is Gibeah. Saul, Israel's king, has two thousand men at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and Jonathan, Saul's son, has a thousand with him in Gibeah of Benjamin (1 Samuel 13:2). I think a thousand men is plenty to keep a commander busy. Hold on to that name, friends, because Jonathan's about to make some noise.

The answer is the Hebrews. Saul blows the ram's horn and says, “Let the Hebrews hear!” He's calling his own people, the people of Israel, and the horn goes out throughout the land. That's one loud announcement, and nobody has to ask what it means.

The answer is Gilgal. The people are summoned to join Saul there (1 Samuel 13:4). Remember that name, friends, because Saul is going to be waiting at Gilgal for a good while. A whole lot of this chapter happens right there.

The answer is False. The Philistines went up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven (1 Samuel 13:5). Gilgal is where the people are summoned to join Saul (1 Samuel 13:4). So the Philistine camp is at Michmash, not at Gilgal.

The answer is that the men of Israel hid in caves and cisterns. The text says they hid in caves and thickets, among the rocks, and in cellars and cisterns, because they saw they were in danger and their troops were hard-pressed. When you're outnumbered like that, any hole in the ground starts looking like a good idea.

The answer is True. The text says, “Saul, however, remained at Gilgal, and all his troops were quaking in fear.” Plenty of people are hiding or leaving, but Saul stays put. That's a lot of shaking going on around one king.

The answer is that the troops begin to desert Saul. He waited seven days for the time appointed by Samuel, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal (1 Samuel 13:8). I think a king watching his army walk off would feel that in his stomach.

The answer is the burnt and peace offerings. Saul says, “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings.” Remember, friends, he's been at Gilgal seven days, waiting. Keep an eye on what happens with the burnt offering.

The answer is False. Saul says, “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings.” and then the text says, “…he offered up the burnt offering.” He doesn't wait for Samuel to arrive. Samuel shows up just as Saul finishes (1 Samuel 13:10).

The answer is that he had not sought the favor of the LORD. Saul tells Samuel, “Now the Philistines will descend upon me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.” Those are his words to Samuel, the prophet. Samuel's answer comes next, and it's a serious one.

The answers are foolishly and command. Samuel, the prophet, declares, “You have acted foolishly…” and he says it straight to Saul, with no wrapping on it. Then he says, “You have not kept the command that the LORD your God gave you…” The text calls it a command, and that's the word Samuel uses. It's a heavy moment, friends, because Saul has run into a line he didn't keep.

The answer is True. Samuel says that if Saul had kept the command, “…the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel for all time.” That tells us what was on the table. It's a sobering line, and Samuel doesn't soften it.

The answer is a man after His own heart. Samuel says, “…the LORD has sought a man after His own heart and appointed him ruler over His people…” The text doesn't give a name here, so I won't either. It's a heavy moment for Saul, because Samuel says his kingdom will not endure.

The answer is about six hundred. Saul numbered the troops who were with him, and it came to about six hundred men (1 Samuel 13:15). That's a long way down from the three thousand he picked at the start. It's a small crowd to bring to a big fight.

The answer is False. Saul and Jonathan are in Geba of Benjamin, “…while the Philistines camped at Michmash.” The text has the Philistines camped there, not heading home. And the raiders are about to go out.

The answer is three. Raiders went out of the Philistine camp in three divisions (1 Samuel 13:17). One headed toward Ophrah, another toward Beth-horon, and the third down the border road. That's three different directions.

The answer is that the Philistines forbade Hebrew swords and spears. The Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears.” So no blacksmith could be found in all the land of Israel. That's a move aimed right at the forge.

The answer is only Saul and Jonathan. On the day of battle, not a sword or spear could be found in the hands of the troops with Saul and Jonathan. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had weapons. That's two people with weapons, friends.
